paragraphs.heading: The cool phase
paragraphs.text: La Niña, Spanish for "The Girl", is the colder partner of El Niño. Both belong to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, a worldwide climate pattern seen as swings in sea surface temperature over the tropical Pacific Ocean. ENSO is one pattern with three phases: neutral, La Niña and El Niño. La Niña and El Niño are opposites, and each is declared only when set ocean and air conditions are met or passed. In earlier times La Niña was also called anti-El Niño, or El Viejo, "the old man".

paragraphs.heading: A Pacific tilted by wind
paragraphs.text: The tropical Pacific is lopsided on average. Its eastern part is about 8–10 °C cooler at the surface than its western part. Strong trade winds near the equator push surface water from east to west, and the sun slowly warms it on the way. Warm water gathers in the west, so the thermocline, the zone of change between warm surface water and cooler deep water, sits about 140 m down there but only about 30 m down in the east.

paragraphs.heading: Why the east stays cold
paragraphs.text: Off the west coast of South America, the trade winds and the Coriolis effect together shove surface water westward. This is called Ekman transport. Colder water from below rises along the edge of the continent to fill the gap. Because the thermocline is shallow there, little separates the cold deep water from the surface, and the east cools. The northward Humboldt Current adds cold water from the Southern Ocean, and with this rising water it keeps the sea off Peru cool.

paragraphs.heading: The air above
paragraphs.text: Above the ocean, the Southern Oscillation is the matching swing in the atmosphere, tied to the changes in sea temperature. Wind, surface air pressure and cloud cover all respond to it. During El Niño, air pressure is unusually high over Indonesia and the western Pacific and unusually low over the eastern Pacific, which is the negative phase. La Niña brings the opposite pattern, called the positive phase.

paragraphs.heading: Cooling the whole planet
paragraphs.text: Where El Niño briefly lifts the global average surface temperature, a La Niña event cools the surface for a short time. So the balance between how often each phase occurs can shape global temperature trends over about ten years. Both phases also disturb normal weather, bringing intense storms to some regions and drought to others. Their strength tends to peak in the northern hemisphere winter, though local effects may peak at other times.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to forecast
paragraphs.text: The Pacific moves between La Niña, El Niño and neutral conditions irregularly, about every two to seven years, with each event differing in strength. ENSO is not easy to predict, but many weather agencies watch it closely. Climate scientists count it as one of the sources of internal climate variability. How it will change as the climate warms is uncertain. Still, the IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report judged in 2021 that over the long term, swings in rainfall tied to ENSO will very likely grow.
